# darkob — complete reference

darkob 1.20.0 — async Python for the Rubika and Shad messaging platforms.

Read this file top to bottom before writing code. It contains curated guidance, the filter catalogue, and all six client APIs with real signatures. Consult llms.txt for documentation pages omitted here.

Hard rules:
- Handlers are `async def name(bot, event)`.
- `event`, never `message`; `event.chat_id`, never `event.chat.id`.
- Filters come from `darkob.bot.filters` and are INSTANTIATED: `IsGroup()`, not `IsGroup`.
- There is no Dispatcher, no message_handler, no aiogram/Pyrogram types.
- Verify client methods in the API below; Bot instance decorators are included.


---
# SOURCE: get-started/installation.md


## Requirements

- Python **3.10 – 3.14** for darkob 1.20.0 Stable and later
- Linux, macOS or Windows

Darkob 0.19.1 is the last release line supporting Python 3.9. It does not
receive the dependency security floor of 1.20.0; use it only when upgrading
Python is not possible.

## Install

```bash
pip install darkob
```

The core install is deliberately small — `aiohttp>=3.14.4,<4`, `aiofiles`
and `pycryptodome`. Nothing else is required, and no method is lost when the
extras are absent.

Optional extras:

```bash
pip install "darkob[speed]"   # msgspec: faster JSON on every update
pip install "darkob[cli]"     # rich: styled console banner and prompts
```

Media metadata (audio duration, image and video dimensions) needs
**no** dependency at all: `darkob.utils.media_parser` reads the
binary headers directly with the standard library. That used to
require `mutagen` plus a temporary file per upload.

Further extras, needed only for specific media features:

```bash
pip install "darkob[opencv]"     # video thumbnails via OpenCV
pip install "darkob[movie]"      # video thumbnails via MoviePy
pip install "darkob[pillow]"     # image thumbnails via Pillow
pip install "darkob[aiortc]"     # voice chats
pip install "darkob[pro]"        # everything above
```

## Verify

```bash
python -c "import darkob; print(darkob.__version__)"
```

Importing darkob performs no network I/O and prints nothing unless you
ask it to.

## Development install

```bash
git clone https://github.com/ManiTheFerfri/darkob.git
cd darkob
pip install -e ".[dev]"

pytest                 # 800+ tests, no network required
ruff check .           # lint
pytest --cov=darkob    # coverage
```

## The banner

`Bot(...)` and `Messenger(...)` print a one-time welcome banner. Disable
it when it would pollute logs:

```python
bot = Bot(token="...", show_welcome=False)
```

## Checking for updates

Never automatic. Call it yourself if you want a notice:

```python
import darkob
darkob.check_for_updates()   # returns the new version string, or None
```


---
# SOURCE: get-started/quickstart.md


## 1. Get a bot token

Create a bot with Rubika's official bot creator and copy the token it
gives you. A valid token looks like 64 uppercase alphanumeric
characters.

## 2. Your first bot

```python
from darkob import Bot

bot = Bot(token="YOUR_BOT_TOKEN")

@bot.on_command("start")
async def start(bot, event):
    await event.reply("Welcome 👋")

@bot.on_new_message()
async def echo(bot, event):
    if not event.text:
        return
    await event.reply(event.text)

bot.run()
```

`bot.run()` starts long polling and blocks until you stop it with Ctrl+C.

## 3. Send messages from a handler

```python
@bot.on_command("hello")
async def hello(bot, event):
    await bot.send_message(event.chat_id, "Hello!")
```

`event` carries the incoming update:

| Attribute | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `event.chat_id` | Conversation to reply in |
| `event.author_id` | User who sent it |
| `event.text` | Message text (`None` when there is none) |
| `event.reply(text)` | Shortcut: send into the same chat |
| `event.forward()`, `event.delete()` | Act on the message |

## 4. Run as a webhook instead

Polling needs no public address; webhooks need one.

```python
bot.run(
    webhook_url="https://example.com/wk",
    host="0.0.0.0",
    port=8080,
)
```

`bot.run()` polls every 50 ms by default, tunable with `poll_interval`.
The lower-level `bot.start()` default is 5 ms.

!!! warning "Always set a webhook secret"
    A webhook URL that leaks lets anyone inject fake updates into
    your bot — a fake `/start`, a fake admin command. darkob cannot
    verify who posted, so agree on a shared secret:

    ```python
    bot = Bot(token="...", webhook_secret="long-random-string")
    bot.run(webhook_url="https://example.com/wk?secret=long-random-string")
    ```

    Requests without a matching `?secret=` or `X-Webhook-Secret`
    header are rejected with `401`. With no secret configured, a
    warning is logged on the first webhook request.

## 5. Tell users what the bot can do

```python
bot.set_commands({
    "start": "Start the bot",
    "help": "Show help",
})
```

## 6. Grow the bot

Once one file stops being enough:

- [Handlers](../guides/handlers.md) — every decorator and what triggers it
- [Filters](../guides/filters.md) — narrow down which events a handler sees
- [Routers](../guides/routers.md) — split handlers into modules
- [Conversations](../guides/fsm.md) — multi-step flows
- [Errors](../guides/errors.md) — stop silent failures

## Async or not?

Every method works both ways. Without `await`, darkob runs the call on a
background loop and returns the result:

```python
bot = Bot(token="YOUR_TOKEN")
me = bot.get_me()          # blocking, returns the result
me = await bot.get_me()    # async, same result
```

Mixing is safe, but pick one style per codebase. See
[Sync and async](../guides/sync-and-async.md).


---
# SOURCE: get-started/migrating-from-maxrubika.md


darkob is a fork of [maxrubika](https://github.com/MEH2RAB/maxrubika).
It keeps the same concepts and most of the same method names, so most
bots port in minutes.

## 1. Change the package name

```bash
pip uninstall maxrubika
pip install darkob
```

```diff
- import maxrubika
- from maxrubika import Bot
+ import darkob
+ from darkob import Bot
```

The exported names are unchanged: `Bot`, `bot`, `Client`, `Messenger`,
`messenger`, `Shad`, `shad`.

## 1b. Or change nothing but the import

If you would rather migrate later, run the existing code through
the compatibility shim — the only change is the import line:

```diff
- from maxrubika import Messenger
+ from darkob.compat.maxrubika import Messenger
```

Everything maxrubika exported is re-exported there, plus the new
darkob APIs, so a half-migrated file still imports cleanly. The
module emits a `DeprecationWarning` on import to remind you it is a
migration aid, not a destination.

## 2. Keep or migrate existing sessions

Existing encrypted `.max` sessions and legacy string sessions remain readable:
darkob tries both the current and legacy decryption keys. Supported older file
formats are migrated without deleting the source file. Bot tokens need no
migration; use the same token.

Keep a backup before testing a migrated account. Re-authentication is only
needed for a corrupt file, a wrong password, or a format the loader does not
support.

## 3. Behaviour that changed

| Area | Change | Action needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Import | No PyPI update check at import | None. Call `darkob.check_for_updates()` if you want it |
| TLS | Verification **on** by default | If you use a proxy that cannot verify upstreams, pass `verify_ssl=False` |
| Errors | Bare `except:` blocks narrowed | Failures you previously never saw may now surface as exceptions — this is intentional |
| Retries | `max_retries` is a per-request budget, not per endpoint | Expect faster failure and fewer duplicate requests |
| Dispatch | Handlers are indexed by update name | None; ordering within a name is preserved |
| Threads | Sync handlers use a bounded executor | None for normal handlers |
| Sessions | Downloads reuse a pooled session | `download_file` now raises `NoConnection` if you never called `start()` |

## 4. New capabilities

- [`Router`](../guides/routers.md) — group handlers into modules
- [`FSMContext`](../guides/fsm.md) — multi-step conversations
- Generated [API reference](../api/bot.md) that matches the runtime

## 5. Verify

```python
import darkob
print(darkob.__version__)   # installed version
```

Then run your bot through its normal path. If something that used to log
and continue now raises, that is the stability work doing its job — open
an issue if the new behaviour is wrong.


---
# SOURCE: upstream-1-18.md


darkob 0.19 merges the feature surface of maxrubika **v1.18.0** while keeping
darkob's transport, dispatch, compatibility and session-safety work.

This is an additive merge. No method that existed in `Bot`, `Messenger` or
`Shad` before it was removed, and every method exposed by the relocated
upstream commit is present. The merged `Messenger` and `Shad` also keep
darkob's `ask()` and `iter_messages()` helpers.

## New surfaces

Three clients can now be imported from `darkob`:

```python
from darkob import RubiAI, RubikaTV, Rubino

ai = RubiAI(auth="...")
posts = Rubino(auth="...")
tv = RubikaTV(auth="...")
```

All of these are optional to import: the root package loads them lazily, so a
bot that only uses `Bot` or `Messenger` does not import the additional
endpoint modules. These aliases also work for compatibility:

- `rubino`
- `RubiAi`, `rubiai`, `RubikaAI`, `RubikaAi`
- `rubikatv`

Each accepts a `Messenger` via `client=`, or creates one from
`session=`/`string_session=`. `auth=` is also supported for the upstream
API-only mode. Wrapper-created clients forward `timeout`, `proxy`,
`max_retries` and TLS settings. A connected client's HTTP pool is reused.

## New Messenger and Shad APIs

Examples of new upstream methods now available:

- `delete_message` and `forward_message`
- `save_message_draft`
- `send_live_location`
- `get_abs_chats`
- `delete_no_access_group_chat`
- `get_wallet_transfer_message` and `send_wallet_transfer_message`
- `on_scheduled_message`

The endpoint directory reorganisation upstream (grouped messages, chats and
settings) is included. See the generated [Rubino](api/rubino.md),
[RubiAI](api/rubiai.md), [RubikaTV](api/rubikatv.md), and
[Messenger](api/messenger.md) references for the actual current signatures.

## Compatibility rules

- The old Bot call style and the new upstream style both work:

  ```python
  await bot.request("POST", "getMe", json={})
  await bot.request(method="getMe", input={})
  await bot.request("getMe", {})
  ```

  All of them share darkob's retries, rate-limiter feedback, metrics and
  plugin hooks. `Bot(as_dict=True)` returns plain dictionaries.

- `Bot.download_file` still returns raw bytes, or base64 when requested.
  Its resumable `Range` behaviour and documented return types did not change
  to match upstream's new `Data` wrapper.

- `Messenger.send_message` accepts its earlier file, base64 and sticker
  parameters. Those calls are routed to `send_file` or the raw sticker path;
  their arguments are not accepted then silently discarded.

- `get_chat_messages` accepts its historic `(chat, max_id, ...)` form, as well
  as the newer direction-first call shape and keyword parameters.

- Live helpers accept either positional order `(access_token, live_id)` or
  `(live_id, access_token)` only when the argument shapes make that
  unambiguous. **Use keywords** for arbitrary strings; tokens beginning with
  nothing recognizable are deliberately left in the legacy order.

- Voice-chat arguments such as `voice_chat_id` are optional for existing
  calls. When absent, the library resolves the current chat's active voice
  chat, or raises `VoiceChatNotActive` rather than inventing one.

## Upstream v1.18.1 refinements

The v1.18.1 patch is included without surrendering darkob's earlier
compatibility work:

- `file_inline` is placed after the older keyword options on all media send
  helpers, restoring their previous positional layout.
- The `base64` argument no longer shadows the decoder module. Malformed
  payloads raise `InvalidInput`; valid line-wrapped base64 still works.
- Missing local media paths are rejected before an upload starts. HTTP(S)
  remote paths still use the pooled session and configured TLS settings.
- `send_video_message` retains the caption and metadata parameters for
  compatibility instead of removing parameters upstream described as unused.
- Rubino keeps one global retry budget while classifying API failures and
  transport failures. `aiohttp.ClientError` and `OSError` can retry, API
  errors cannot hide inside that retry loop merely because their text mentions
  a network problem.
- RubiAI retries server-side `503`/`502`/`500`/`504` response failures and
  does not retry client errors such as `400`.
- Generated-image downloads accept `pathlib.Path` and raise deliberately when
  a `Success` response contains no image data.

## Sessions are not reset by the merge

Existing darkob sessions remain `.max` files at their stable paths. The
primary database key and the current `StringSession` secret are unchanged.
Migration is read-compatible:

- older maxrubika database encryption keys are accepted while reading;
- upstream `StringSession` secrets are accepted when no explicit password is
  supplied;
- supplied passwords are never bypassed by fallback secrets;
- source session files are **not deleted** after migration;
- unreadable files are still quarantined rather than destroyed.

Use your usual `session=` or `string_session=` value. There is no mandatory
re-login step.

## Transport and async changes retained or added

- Rubino uses one retry budget for a whole request instead of allowing
  `max_retries` attempts for every one of 85 candidate URLs.
- The new surfaces reuse connected sessions when available and verify TLS by
  default. `verify_ssl=False` is still available explicitly; it is not forced.
- `proxy` and `timeout` are forwarded by Rubino, RubiAI and RubikaTV.
- Media thumbnail and audio parsing is moved off the event loop in the new
  send paths, and rubino disk reads/writes use `aiofiles`.
- Timestamp defaults such as `round(time()) - 150` are evaluated per request,
  not frozen when Python imports the module.

## Verification

The merge includes coverage for both historical call shapes and the new
surfaces: import and API retention checks, session key compatibility,
`Data` indexing with nested `Data` objects, mock HTTP transport and TLS
settings, bounded retries, raw sticker payloads, voice/live compatibility and
update-timestamp behaviour. No live endpoint was needed for these tests; the
new APIs' presence and signatures are additionally checked against the
relocated upstream source.

See also:

- [Migrating from maxrubika](get-started/migrating-from-maxrubika.md)
- [Bot vs Messenger vs Shad](explanation/bot-vs-messenger-vs-shad.md)
- [Reliability](explanation/reliability.md)

# SOURCE: tutorials/first-bot.md


A hands-on walkthrough that ends with a bot which echoes, answers one command, and puts a working button under a message.

## 1. Install

```bash
pip install darkob
```

darkob 1.20.0+ needs Python 3.10 or newer. Confirm the install:

```bash
python -c "import darkob; print(darkob.__version__)"
```

Importing darkob performs no network I/O, so this works offline.

## 2. Get a bot token

Create a bot with Rubika's official bot creator and copy the token it
shows you. A token is 64 characters: five uppercase letters, then 59
characters that are digits or uppercase letters.

!!! warning "The token is a password"
    Anyone holding it can send messages as your bot. Keep it out of the
    repository and read it from the environment instead:

    ```python
    import os
    token = os.environ["RUBIKA_BOT_TOKEN"]
    ```

## 3. A bot that echoes messages

Create `bot.py`:

```python title="bot.py"
from darkob import Bot

bot = Bot(token="YOUR_BOT_TOKEN")

@bot.on_new_message()
async def echo(bot, event):
    if not event.text:
        return
    await event.reply(event.text)

bot.run()
```

`Bot(...)` validates the token and creates its handler registry; the HTTP
session is opened on first use. `bot.run()` then starts long polling and
blocks until you stop it.

Run it and send the bot any message:

```bash
python bot.py
```

A one-time banner appears, then `Bot started in polling mode...`. The bot
answers with the same text you sent. Stop it with Ctrl+C.

A handler is a plain async function taking two arguments: the bot, and the
event. `event.text` holds the message text, or `None` when the update
carries none, and `event.reply(text)` sends into the same chat as a
threaded reply.

!!! note "A mistyped token does not raise"
    If the token does not match the expected shape, `Bot(...)` asks for
    one interactively in the terminal. A prompt in the middle of a
    deployment log means the token was wrong, not missing.

## 4. Only answer commands

Echoing everything is rarely useful. A filter decides whether a handler
runs, so add one:

```python title="bot.py"
from darkob import Bot
from darkob.bot.filters import Command

bot = Bot(token="YOUR_BOT_TOKEN")

@bot.on_new_message(Command("echo"))
async def echo(bot, event):
    await event.reply(event.command_args or "nothing to echo")

bot.run()
```

Now `/echo hello` replies `hello`, while a plain `hello` is ignored. The
filter matches `/echo` and `/echo@your_bot`, and lets every other command
fall through to other handlers.

`event.command_args` is everything after the command, or `""`.

!!! tip "One decorator instead of two filters"
    `@bot.on_command("echo")` applies the message and command filters for
    you, and takes a list: `@bot.on_command(["echo", "بازگو"])`. Once your
    bot has several commands, that shortcut keeps the code shorter.

## 5. Add an inline keyboard button

Buttons live under the message, so they need an inline keypad. Give each
button an `id`; that id is what comes back when somebody presses it.

```python title="bot.py"
from darkob import Bot, Button, Keyboard

bot = Bot(token="YOUR_BOT_TOKEN")

@bot.on_command("menu")
async def menu(bot, event):
    keypad = Keyboard().row(
        Button("Say hi", id="hi"),
        Button("Docs", id="docs"),
    )
    await bot.send_message(event.chat_id, "Pick one:", inline_keypad=keypad)

@bot.on_callback()
async def on_button(bot, event):
    if event.button_id == "hi":
        await event.reply("Hi there 👋")
    else:
        await event.reply("Docs: https://github.com/ManiTheFerfri/darkob")

bot.run()
```

A press arrives as an `InlineMessage` update, and `@bot.on_callback()`
fires on exactly that. `event.button_id` holds the `id` you set, and
`event.reply(...)` still works because the payload carries the chat and
message it belongs to.

Buttons without an explicit `id` get a numeric one assigned for you
(`"100"`, `"101"`, …). That is fine for a static menu, but an explicit id
is what makes the handler readable.

## 6. Run it

The finished file:

```python title="bot.py"
import os

from darkob import Bot, Button, Keyboard
from darkob.bot.filters import Command

bot = Bot(token=os.environ["RUBIKA_BOT_TOKEN"])

@bot.on_new_message(Command("echo"))
async def echo(bot, event):
    await event.reply(event.command_args or "nothing to echo")

@bot.on_command("menu")
async def menu(bot, event):
    keypad = Keyboard().row(
        Button("Say hi", id="hi"),
        Button("Docs", id="docs"),
    )
    await bot.send_message(event.chat_id, "Pick one:", inline_keypad=keypad)

@bot.on_callback()
async def on_button(bot, event):
    if event.button_id == "hi":
        await event.reply("Hi there 👋")
    else:
        await event.reply("Docs: https://github.com/ManiTheFerfri/darkob")

bot.run()
```

```bash
python bot.py
```

Send `/echo hi`, then `/menu` and press a button. Both handlers fire, in
that order of registration, for events that match them.

## Where to go next

- More decorators and middleware: [Handlers](../guides/handlers.md)
- Narrow handlers by chat, media or text: [Filters](../guides/filters.md)
- Every button type the API accepts: [Keyboards and formatting](../guides/keyboards.md)
- Multi-step conversations: [Conversations (FSM)](../guides/fsm.md)
- Test all of this without a token: [Testing without a token](testing-without-a-token.md)

- [Quickstart](../get-started/quickstart.md)

# SOURCE: guides/handlers.md


A handler is an async (or plain) function registered on the bot. darkob
calls it as `handler(bot, event)` when a matching update arrives.

## Decorators

All decorators are available on a `Bot` instance.

| Decorator | Fires on |
| --- | --- |
| `@bot.on_new_message()` | Brand-new messages |
| `@bot.on_edit_message()` | Edited messages |
| `@bot.on_delete_message()` | Deleted messages |
| `@bot.on_message()` | Any of new / edit / delete / inline |
| `@bot.on_callback()` | Inline keyboard clicks |
| `@bot.on_command("start")` | Messages that start with a command |
| `@bot.on_update()` | **Any** update the server sends |
| `@bot.on_event_data()` | System events (joins, leaves, pins, …) |
| `@bot.on_bot_joined()` | Bot added to a chat |
| `@bot.on_bot_removed()` | Bot removed from a chat |
| `@bot.on_bot_permissions_changed()` | Bot rights changed |
| `@bot.on_started_bot()` / `@bot.on_stopped_bot()` | Bot lifecycle on the server |
| `@bot.on_start()` / `@bot.on_shutdown()` | Your process starting / stopping |

## Basic handler

```python
@bot.on_new_message()
async def echo(bot, event):
    await event.reply(event.text)
```

## Adding constraints

Every decorator accepts constraints, which decide whether the handler
runs. They compose with `&`, `|` and `~`.

```python
from darkob.bot.filters import IsGroup, IsImage

@bot.on_new_message(IsGroup(), IsImage())
async def group_photo(bot, event):
    await event.reply("Nice picture")
```

See [Filters](filters.md) for the full list.

## Commands

```python
@bot.on_command("start")
@bot.on_command(["start", "begin", "شروع"])
@bot.on_command()                       # any command
@bot.on_command("help", prefixes=["/", "!"])
```

## Editing a message

```python
await bot.edit_message(
    event.chat_id,
    event.message_id,
    "Updated text",
    inline_keypad=Keyboard().row("Done"),
)
```

The inline keypad is optional; omit it to leave the existing buttons
alone.

## Middleware

A middleware wraps dispatch. Call `call_next()` to continue, or return
without calling it to stop the chain.

```python
@bot.middleware()
async def log_everything(bot, event, call_next):
    print("incoming:", getattr(event, "text", ""))
    await call_next()
```

Middlewares run in registration order, outermost first.

## Ordering and stopping

By default every matching handler runs, in registration order. Set
`run_all_handlers=False` on the bot to run only the first match:

```python
bot = Bot(token="...", run_all_handlers=False)
```

A handler that raises does not stop the others; the exception is logged.

## Lifecycle hooks

```python
@bot.on_start()
async def warm_up(bot):
    print("bot is starting")

@bot.on_shutdown()
async def clean_up(bot):
    print("bot is stopping")
```

## Sync handlers

A plain function works too — it is executed in a bounded thread pool so
it cannot block the event loop:

```python
@bot.on_command("ping")
def ping(bot, event):
    bot.send_message(event.chat_id, "pong")
```


---
# SOURCE: guides/filters.md


Filters decide whether a handler runs. Import them from
`darkob.bot.filters`.

```python
from darkob.bot.filters import IsGroup, Text, IsImage
```

## Composing

Filters combine with Python operators: `&` (both), `|` (either), `~` (not).

```python
@bot.on_new_message(IsGroup() & ~IsImage())
async def text_in_group(bot, event):
    ...
```

Precedence follows Python: `~` binds tighter than `&`, which binds
tighter than `|`.

## Message shape

| Filter | Matches |
| --- | --- |
| `IsMessage()` | A new message |
| `IsEdited()` | An edit |
| `IsDeleted()` | A deletion |
| `IsCallback()` | An inline keyboard callback |
| `IsStartedBot()` / `IsStoppedBot()` | Bot lifecycle updates |
| `IsEventData()` | System event payloads |

## Text

| Filter | Matches |
| --- | --- |
| `Text("hello")` | Text containing the pattern (regex) |
| `TextMatch(r"name: (\w+)")` | Same, and stores the match on `event.pattern_match` |
| `Command("start")` | A command, optionally with a bot suffix |
| `IsText()` | Any text message |

```python
@bot.on_new_message(TextMatch(r"order\s+(\d+)"))
async def order(bot, event):
    number = event.pattern_match.group(1)
    await event.reply(f"Order #{number}")
```

## Chat kind

| Filter | Matches |
| --- | --- |
| `IsUser()` | A direct chat |
| `IsGroup()` | A group |
| `IsChannel()` | A channel |
| `ChatType("Group")` | By explicit type name |
| `FromChat("g0…")` | A specific chat |
| `FromUser("u0…")` | A specific user |

## Media

`IsFile()`, `IsImage()`, `IsVideo()`, `IsVoice()`, `IsMusic()`,
`IsSticker()`, `IsPoll()`, `IsLocation()`, `IsReply()`,
`IsForwarded()`.

Forward details: `ForwardedFromUser()`, `ForwardedFromChannel()`,
`ForwardedFromBot()`, `ForwardedNoLink()`.

## Formatting metadata

| Filter | Matches |
| --- | --- |
| `HasMetadata()` | Text carrying bold/italic/link formatting |
| `MetadataType("Bold")` | A specific metadata type |

## Membership and rights

| Filter | Matches |
| --- | --- |
| `IsJoined()` | The bot/user is a member |
| `IsAdmin()` | Admin rights |
| `IsOwner()` | Ownership |

## Events

```python
from darkob.bot.filters import EventType

@bot.on_event_data(EventType("AddedGroupMembers"))
async def someone_joined(bot, event):
    await event.reply("Welcome to the group!")
```

## Writing your own

Subclass `EventConstraint` and implement `evaluate`:

```python
from darkob.bot.filters import EventConstraint

class IsLongMessage(EventConstraint):
    def __init__(self, minimum: int = 500):
        self.minimum = minimum

    async def evaluate(self, event) -> bool:
        return len(getattr(event, "text", "") or "") >= self.minimum
```

`evaluate` may be async and may do I/O. A filter that raises is treated
as "no match" and the error is logged.


---
# SOURCE: guides/routers.md


A `Router` collects handlers without needing a bot instance, then
registers them all at once. Use it to split a bot into feature modules.

## Basic use

```python
from darkob import Bot, Router

bot = Bot(token="YOUR_BOT_TOKEN")
admin = Router("admin")

@admin.command("ban")
async def ban(bot, event):
    await bot.ban_member(event.chat_id, event.author_id)
    await event.reply("Banned.")

bot.include_router(admin)
bot.run()
```

## Why bother

- Handlers live next to the feature they implement, in their own file.
- A module can be tested without a token.
- Nested routers let one root assemble the whole bot.

## Nesting

```python
root = Router("root")
admin = Router("admin")
moderation = Router("moderation")

admin.include_router(moderation)
root.include_router(admin)

bot.include_router(root)     # registers everything, recursively
```

`len(router)` counts all routes including children.

## Router decorators

Mirror the bot decorators exactly:

`update()`, `message()`, `new_message()`, `edit_message()`,
`delete_message()`, `callback()`, `command()`, `event_data()`.

```python
@router.command("start")
@router.command(["help", "?", "راهنما"])
@router.message(IsGroup())
```

Constraints are passed through unchanged, so a router route behaves
identically to the same decorator written on the bot.

## Router middleware

A middleware declared on a router wraps **only** that router's
handlers, including routers nested inside it.

```python
@router.middleware()
async def log(bot, event, call_next):
    print("before")
    await call_next()
    print("after")
```

Call `await call_next()` to continue; return without calling it to
stop the handler. Multiple middlewares run outermost-first.

## Inspecting a router

```python
router.routes      # routes declared directly on this router
router.children    # nested routers
len(router)        # total routes, recursively
router.apply(bot)  # register manually; returns the number registered
```

## Registration rules

- `include_router` returns the router, so calls chain.
- Including the same child twice is a no-op.
- A router cannot include itself (`ValueError`).
- `bot.include_router(obj)` raises `TypeError` if `obj` is not a `Router`.
- Handlers register in declaration order; middleware, if any, is bot-level.

## Testing a router without a token

```python
router = Router()

@router.command("ping")
async def ping(bot, event):
    ...

assert len(router) == 1
assert router.routes[0].kind == "on_command"
```


---
# SOURCE: guides/fsm.md


A finite state machine tracks which step a user is on, and what they have
already told you.

## The idea

Two pieces of data per conversation:

- **state** — a string like `"waiting_for_address"`, or `None`
- **data** — a free-form dict

Both live in a `Storage`, keyed by chat (or user) id.

## Complete example

```python
from darkob import Bot, FSMContext, JsonFileStorage, StateFilter

bot = Bot(token="YOUR_BOT_TOKEN")
storage = JsonFileStorage("fsm.json")   # survives restarts

@bot.on_command("order")
async def order(bot, event):
    ctx = FSMContext(storage, key=event.chat_id)
    await ctx.set_state("address")
    await event.reply("What is your delivery address?")

@bot.on_new_message(StateFilter(storage, "address"))
async def address(bot, event):
    ctx = FSMContext(storage, key=event.chat_id)
    await ctx.update_data(address=event.text)
    await ctx.clear()
    await event.reply("Order received ✅")
```

The second handler only runs while the conversation is in the `address`
state, so it will not hijack unrelated messages.

## Storage backends

| Storage | Survives restart | Use for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MemoryStorage()` | No | Tests, ephemeral bots |
| `JsonFileStorage("fsm.json")` | Yes | Single-process bots |
| `TTLMemoryStorage(ttl=3600)` | No | State that should expire |
| `SQLiteStorage("fsm.db")` | Yes | Durable and concurrency-safe |

`JsonFileStorage` writes atomically, tolerates a corrupt file (it starts
empty rather than crashing), and is safe to call from concurrent tasks.
`SQLiteStorage` runs in WAL mode, so it survives a hard kill mid-write
and is safe for several tasks writing at once.

```python
from darkob import SQLiteStorage, TTLMemoryStorage

storage = SQLiteStorage("darkob_fsm.db")   # durable
storage = TTLMemoryStorage(ttl=1800)         # forgets after 30 min
```

## FSMContext

```python
ctx = FSMContext(storage, key="g0abc")          # explicit key
ctx = FSMContext.from_event(storage, event)     # key from the event

await ctx.get_state()                # str | None
await ctx.set_state("waiting")
await ctx.set_state(None)            # clear the state

await ctx.get_data()                 # dict
await ctx.set_data({"a": 1})         # replace
await ctx.update_data(a=2, b=3)      # merge, returns the new dict
await ctx.clear()                    # state + data
```

## StateFilter

```python
StateFilter(storage, "address")
StateFilter(storage, "address", key_func=lambda e: e.author_id)
```

It is a normal filter, so it composes:

```python
from darkob.bot.filters import IsGroup

@bot.on_new_message(IsGroup() & StateFilter(storage, "address"))
async def group_address(bot, event):
    ...
```

## Choosing a key

`default_storage_key` prefers `chat_id`, then `object_guid`, then
`author_object_guid`, falling back to `"default"`.

Use a custom key to scope a conversation per user instead of per chat:

```python
ctx = FSMContext(storage, key=f"order:{event.author_id}")
```

## Custom storage

Implement `Storage` to back it with Redis or SQL:

```python
from darkob import Storage

class RedisStorage(Storage):
    async def get_state(self, key): ...
    async def set_state(self, key, state): ...
    async def get_data(self, key): ...
    async def set_data(self, key, data): ...
```

The four methods are all you need; `clear()` and `close()` have default
implementations.


---
# SOURCE: guides/inline-conversations.md


Two ways to ask a user something without writing a state machine.

## `ask()` — wait for the next reply

```python
from darkob import Bot, NoReply

bot = Bot(token="...")

@bot.on_command("signup")
async def signup(bot, event):
    await event.reply("What is your name?")

    try:
        reply = await bot.ask(event.chat_id, timeout=60)
    except NoReply:
        await event.reply("Never mind.")
        return

    await event.reply(f"Nice to meet you, {reply.text}")
```

While the prompt is pending, the next message in that chat is handed to
**you** instead of being dispatched to handlers, so no `waiting_for = True`
flag is needed.

### With a prompt and filters

```python
reply = await bot.ask(
    event.chat_id,
    "Send me a photo",
    filters=[lambda ev: ev.text and ev.text.startswith("/")],
    timeout=30,
)
```

The `text` argument is optional — pass it to send the question for you:

```python
reply = await bot.ask(event.chat_id, "Pick one", inline_keypad=Keyboard().row("A", "B"))
```

Both surfaces support it: `bot.ask(...)` and `client.ask(...)`.

| Behaviour | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Timeout | Raises `darkob.NoReply` (a `TimeoutError` subclass) |
| Queueing | Two pending asks in one chat are served oldest-first |
| Filters | Each is called with the event; sync or async, exceptions count as "no match" |
| Cleanup | The waiter is removed on success, timeout or cancellation |

## `StatesGroup` — named states

Plain strings work, but a class keeps them together and typo-free:

```python
from darkob import FSMContext, JsonFileStorage, State, StateFilter, StatesGroup

storage = JsonFileStorage("fsm.json")

class Form(StatesGroup):
    name = State()
    email = State()

@bot.on_command("register")
async def register(bot, event):
    ctx = FSMContext(storage, key=event.chat_id)
    await ctx.set_state(Form.name)
    await event.reply("Name?")

@bot.on_new_message(StateFilter(storage, Form.name))
async def got_name(bot, event):
    ctx = FSMContext(storage, key=event.chat_id)
    await ctx.update_data(name=event.text)
    await ctx.set_state(Form.email)
    await event.reply("Email?")
```

`State` is a `str` subclass ordered by its group, so it flows through
every existing helper — storage backends, `StateFilter`, and comparisons —
with no changes:

```python
Form.name == "Form.name"      # True
Form.states()                 # {"name": State('Form.name'), ...}
list(Form.values())           # ["Form.name", "Form.other"]
```

Two groups cannot collide: `Form.name` and `Survey.name` are different
state strings.

## Which to use

| Need | Use |
| --- | --- |
| One question, then continue | `ask()` |
| Several steps, resumable after a restart | `StatesGroup` + `FSMContext` |
| Steps that must survive the process | FSM with `JsonFileStorage` or `SQLiteStorage` |


---
# SOURCE: guides/keyboards.md


Two helpers remove most of the boilerplate from bot code: keypad
builders, and text formatting.

## Keypads

A :class:`Keyboard` **is** a dict (`{"rows": [...]}`), so it can be passed
anywhere the API accepts a raw keypad. Ids and button types are filled in
automatically.

```python
from darkob import Keyboard

keypad = Keyboard().row("Yes", "No").row("Cancel")

await bot.send_message(chat_id, "Continue?", inline_keypad=keypad)
```

Chat keyboards (the persistent bottom keyboard) use the same builder:

```python
await bot.send_message(chat_id, "Menu", chat_keypad=Keyboard().row("Help", "Settings"))
```

### Chaining

```python
(
    Keyboard()                # empty
    .row("A", "B")            # one row, two buttons
    .row("C")                 # second row
    .button("Alone")          # a row with a single button
    .clear()                  # remove all rows
)
```

Inspect before sending:

```python
keyboard.row_count        # number of rows
keyboard.button_count     # total buttons
keyboard.to_dict()        # plain-dict copy
Keyboard.from_rows([["A", "B"], ["C"]])
```

### Explicit buttons

```python
from darkob import Button

Button("Delete", id=42, type="Selection")

Keyboard().row(
    Button("Delete", id=42, type="Selection"),
    "Plain string button",
    {"button_text": "Raw dict", "type": "Simple"},
)
```

`Button` accepts `text`, `id`, `type` and any extra keyword fields, which
are forwarded to the API verbatim:

```python
Button("Open", url="https://example.com")
```

An empty button label raises `ValueError` immediately instead of failing
server-side.

### With the Messenger surface

The userbot `send_message` takes `inline_keypad` and `chat_keypad` too,
and accepts the same `Keyboard`.

## Text formatting

Rubika renders a small Markdown dialect. These helpers produce it exactly:

| Helper | Output |
| --- | --- |
| `bold("x")` | `**x**` |
| `italic("x")` | `__x__` |
| `strike("x")` | `~~x~~` |
| `underline("x")` | `--x--` |
| `spoiler("x")` | `\|\|x\|\|` |
| `code("x")` | `` `x` `` |
| `pre("x", "python")` | fenced block |
| `link("text", url)` | `[text](url)` |
| `join([...])` | skips empty fragments |

```python
from darkob import bold, code, link

await event.reply(
    f"{bold('Deployed')} {code('v0.2.1')} — {link('logs', 'https://example.com')}"
)
```

They return plain strings, so they compose inside f-strings and nest:

```python
bold(f"{italic('nested')} works")
```

`link()` raises `ValueError` on an empty URL rather than sending a
malformed message.

## Button types

The Bot API documents 19 button types. Every one has a builder, and the
fields each builder sends are the ones the reference lists — nothing is
invented.

```python
from darkob import Button, Keyboard

keypad = (
    Keyboard()
    .row(Button.simple("Plain"), Button.link("Docs", "https://rubika.ir"))
    .row(Button.selection("Pick", title="Choose", items=[{"text": "A"}]))
    .row(Button.calendar("Date", min_year=2024, max_year=2030))
)
```

| Builder | `type` sent | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Button.simple(text)` | `Simple` | |
| `Button.link(text, url)` | `Link` | |
| `Button.selection(text, title=, items=, columns_count=, is_multi_selection=)` | `Selection` | |
| `Button.calendar(text, title=, min_year=, max_year=)` | `Calendar` | Persian/Gregorian field is not named in the reference |
| `Button.number_picker(text, title=, min_value=, max_value=)` | `NumberPicker` | |
| `Button.string_picker(text, title=, items=)` | `StringPicker` | |
| `Button.location(text, image_url=)` | `Location` | |
| `Button.text_box(text)` | `Textbox` | |
| `Button.ask_my_phone(text)` / `Button.ask_my_location(text)` | `AskMyPhoneNumber` / `AskMyLocation` | |
| `Button.barcode(text)` | `Barcode` | |
| `Button.payment(text, **fields)` | `Payment` | **Requires** extra fields; a bare one is rejected by the API |
| `Button.of("CameraImage", text)` | any | Escape hatch for the remaining types |

All 19 documented types have builders. `Button.payment` raises `ValueError`
locally when required fields are missing, so that malformed request fails
before any network call. Server acceptance still requires a live check.

## Enums

The documented enums live in `darkob.bot.models`, and the common ones are
also exported from the package root:

```python
from darkob import ButtonType, ChatType, FileType
from darkob.bot.models import ChatKeypadType, PollStatus, EventType

FileType.Voice          # "Voice"
ButtonType.Selection    # "Selection"
```

They subclass `str`, so they serialise to the exact wire value and compare
equal to plain strings.

## Putting them together

```python
from darkob import Bot, Keyboard, bold

bot = Bot(token="...")

@bot.on_command("order")
async def order(bot, event):
    keypad = Keyboard().row("Confirm", "Cancel")
    await bot.send_message(
        event.chat_id,
        f"{bold('Order #42')}\nShall I confirm?",
        inline_keypad=keypad,
    )
```


---
# SOURCE: guides/composing-messages.md


Two helpers keep message code short: a builder for the message itself, and
formatting helpers for the text.

## MessageBuilder

Handlers often assemble the same pieces — text, a keypad, a reply target,
a silent flag. The builder keeps them in one place and emits only the
options you actually set.

```python
from darkob import Keyboard, MessageBuilder

message = (
    MessageBuilder("Order #42 confirmed")
    .append("Delivery tomorrow between 9 and 12")
    .inline(Keyboard().row("Track", "Cancel"))
    .silent()
)

await message.send(bot, event.chat_id)
```

### Building text

```python
builder = MessageBuilder("Line one")
builder.append("Line two")        # newline separated
builder.line()                    # blank line
builder.line("After the gap")
builder.set_text("Start over")    # replace everything

builder.text                      # the string so far
len(builder)                      # character count
```

`append` takes any separator:

```python
MessageBuilder("a").append("b", separator=" ·  ").text   # "a · b"
```

### Options

| Method | Sets |
| --- | --- |
| `.keypad(kb)` | `chat_keypad` — the persistent bottom keyboard |
| `.inline(kb)` | `inline_keypad` — buttons attached to the message |
| `.reply_to(message_id)` | `reply_to_message_id` |
| `.silent()` | `disable_notification` |
| `.metadata(meta)` | Rubika text metadata |
| `.option(name, value)` | Any other `send_message` keyword |
| `.clear_options()` | Drops every option, keeps the text |

### Sending or inspecting

```python
message.build()          # {"text": ..., **options}
await message.send(bot, chat_id)
```

`build()` is plain data, so it is easy to assert on in tests:

```python
assert MessageBuilder("hi").silent().build() == {
    "text": "hi",
    "disable_notification": True,
}
```

## Formatting

| Helper | Output |
| --- | --- |
| `bold("x")` | `**x**` |
| `italic("x")` | `__x__` |
| `strike("x")` | `~~x~~` |
| `underline("x")` | `--x--` |
| `spoiler("x")` | `\|\|x\|\|` |
| `code("x")` | `` `x` `` |
| `pre("x", "python")` | fenced block |
| `link("text", url)` | `[text](url)` |
| `join([...])` | skips empty fragments |

```python
from darkob import bold, code, link

await event.reply(f"{bold('Done')} in {code('1.2s')} — {link('logs', url)}")
```

## Both together

```python
from darkob import Keyboard, MessageBuilder, bold

message = (
    MessageBuilder(bold("Deployment finished"))
    .append("All checks passed")
    .inline(Keyboard().row("View logs", "Roll back"))
    .reply_to(event.message_id)
)

await message.send(bot, event.chat_id)
```


---
# SOURCE: guides/errors.md


darkob raises typed exceptions instead of returning `None` and hoping.

## Bot API exceptions

Import from `darkob.bot.exceptions`. All inherit from `APIException`.

| Exception | Raised when |
| --- | --- |
| `Network` | The request could not complete after the retry budget |
| `Timeout` | The request or the server timed out |
| `BadGateway` | Upstream returned HTTP 502 |
| `ServerError` | Server-side failure (`SERVER_ERROR`) |
| `JSONDecode` | The response body was not valid JSON |
| `InvalidResponse` | Unexpected response shape |
| `InvalidInput` | The request was rejected (`INVALID_INPUT`) |
| `InvalidAccess` | Not authorised (`INVALID_ACCESS`) |
| `TooRequests` | Rate limited (`TOO_REQUESTS`) |
| `TokenError` | The bot token is malformed |

```python
from darkob.bot.exceptions import TooRequests, Network

try:
    await bot.send_message(chat_id, "hi")
except TooRequests:
    await asyncio.sleep(5)
except Network:
    log.warning("network down, giving up on this message")
```

## Messenger exceptions

| Exception | Raised when |
| --- | --- |
| `NetworkError` | Could not reach a data centre |
| `RequestError` | The API rejected the request |
| `ValidationError` | Bad argument passed by you |
| `InvalidInput`, `InvalidAccess`, `TooRequests`, `ServerError` | API-level statuses |
| `AuthError`, `SessionError`, `ApiVersionError`, `PlatformError` | Construction / login problems |
| `TimeoutError`, `MaxRetriesError`, `ProxyError` | Configuration problems |
| `NoConnection` | You called a method before `start()` |

## Retries

`max_retries` is a **budget for one request**, not per endpoint.

- Attempts rotate across known data-centre endpoints before repeating.
- Backoff carries jitter, so many bots do not retry in lockstep.
- HTTP `429` and a `TOO_REQUESTS` payload get a longer, escalating delay.
- The endpoint that answered last is promoted for the next request.

```python
bot = Bot(token="...", max_retries=3)     # 3 attempts total
```

Set `max_retries=0` to fail fast in tests.

## Surviving a bad connection

`SendQueue` wraps sending so a dropped connection does not lose
messages:

```python
from darkob import Bot, SendQueue

bot = Bot(token="...")
queue = SendQueue(bot, path="outbox.json")   # survives a restart
queue.start()                                  # flush in the background

await queue.put(event.chat_id, "report ready")
```

`put` returns `True` when the message went out immediately and
`False` when it was queued. Only transient failures (network,
timeout) are queued; a permanent error such as an invalid chat id
is raised at once, and is dropped during a flush rather than
blocking everything behind it.

## Bounding concurrency

Inbound updates run as background tasks under a semaphore, so a
burst cannot create unbounded work:

```python
bot = Bot(token="...", max_concurrent_updates=16)
```

The default is 32. The same limit applies to the Messenger
WebSocket path.

## Tracking protocol drift

Rubika reshuffles its data-centre endpoints from time to time. A tracker
makes that visible instead of mysterious:

```python
from darkob import ProtocolTracker

tracker = ProtocolTracker(path="protocol.json")
changes = tracker.record(client.connection, client)
if changes:
    print("protocol changed:", changes)
```

It snapshots the API and socket URLs, the endpoint codes, the platform and
the app version, stores the last snapshot, and reports differences.

## Rate limiting

Rubika throttles bots, and a burst of sends is the fastest way to
earn a `TOO_REQUESTS`. A limiter keeps you under the ceiling before
the server has to enforce it.

```python
from darkob import Bot, RateLimiter

bot = Bot(
    token="...",
    rate_limiter=RateLimiter(rate=20, burst=5, per_chat_rate=3),
)
```

`rate` is tokens per second, `burst` the bucket size. With
`per_chat_rate`, each conversation gets its own bucket so one busy
group cannot starve the rest; the buckets are capped and evicted
oldest-first, so memory stays bounded.

The limiter applies to every attempt, including retries.

## Circuit breaker

Each data-centre endpoint has its own breaker. After 5 consecutive
failures it opens, and requests stop being sent to that endpoint
for 30 seconds. After the timeout it half-opens and one request is
allowed through as a probe; success closes it, failure reopens it.

This stops a dead endpoint from consuming the retry budget of every
request. The class is darkob.CircuitBreaker, and each connection
keeps one per endpoint:

```python
client.connection.breaker_for("https://api.example")
breaker.threshold = 10        # be more tolerant
breaker.reset_timeout = 60.0  # wait longer before probing
```

If every endpoint is open, the request fails immediately with a log
line instead of timing out.

## Retry policy

For anything more than a count, pass a :class:`Retry` policy. It
overrides `max_retries` on both the Bot and Messenger surfaces.

```python
from darkob import Retry

bot = Bot(token="...", retry=Retry(attempts=5, backoff=0.5))
bot = Bot(token="...", retry=Retry.none())        # fail fast
bot = Bot(token="...", retry=Retry.patient())     # few, slow tries
bot = Bot(token="...", retry=Retry.aggressive())  # many, quick tries
```

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `attempts` | Total attempts, including the first |
| `backoff` | Base delay in seconds, growing linearly |
| `jitter` | Fraction of the delay randomised (0–1) |
| `max_delay` | Ceiling for any single wait |
| `rate_limit_backoff` | Base delay when the server reports rate limiting |

`Retry.delay(attempt)` and `Retry.should_retry(attempt)` are pure
functions, so they are easy to unit test.

## What darkob does not do

- It never swallows `KeyboardInterrupt` or `SystemExit` — only `Exception`.
- It retries only `429` among client errors; other `4xx` responses are your bug.
- It does not hide handler crashes: a failing handler is logged with a
  traceback and the remaining handlers still run.

## Debugging a silent bot

1. Turn on logging:

   ```python
   import logging
   logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG)
   ```

2. Check that your filter actually matches — log inside the handler.
3. Check the bot token and chat id.
4. If nothing is delivered at all, switch to polling to rule out the
   webhook path.


---
# SOURCE: guides/sync-and-async.md


Every public method exists in both flavours.

## The rule

- Called with `await` → runs on the current event loop.
- Called without `await` → darkob submits the coroutine to one shared
  background loop and blocks until it returns.

```python
me = await bot.get_me()     # async
me = bot.get_me()           # sync, same result
```

## How it works

`darkob.hybrid` starts one daemon thread when the first sync call is
made. That thread owns an asyncio loop; sync calls hand work to it with
`run_coroutine_threadsafe` and wait. There is no per-call thread, and the
loop is shut down at interpreter exit.

## Choosing a style

| Style | Use when |
| --- | --- |
| `async` | You already run a loop, or you need concurrency |
| `sync` | A script, a cron job, a quick prototype |

Pick one per codebase. Inside a running event loop, a hybrid method returns
a coroutine just like any other `async def`: if you do not `await` it, it does
not execute. Use `await` inside async handlers.

## Calling sync code inside an async handler

If you must, hand it to a thread so the loop keeps running:

```python
import asyncio

@bot.on_command("report")
async def report(bot, event):
    await asyncio.to_thread(bot.get_me)      # sync form in a separate thread
```

Prefer rewriting the call as `await`.

## Comparing with the original library

maxrubika derived sync behaviour from the same idea. darkob additionally:

- uses a **bounded** executor for blocking handlers, so a burst of events
  cannot spawn unbounded OS threads;
- rejects a sync call made from inside the worker thread itself (it would
  deadlock otherwise) with a clear `RuntimeError`.

## Shutting down

```python
from darkob.hybrid import close_sync_loop

close_sync_loop()    # optional; also runs at exit
```

Long-running processes rarely need this. Tests that use the sync API
should close the loop so the interpreter exits promptly.


---
# SOURCE: guides/testing.md


darkob's own suite runs entirely offline — no sockets, no tokens. You can
do the same for your bot.

## Install the test extras

```bash
pip install pytest pytest-asyncio
```

```ini
# pyproject.toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
asyncio_mode = "auto"
```

## Test a handler without a bot

Handlers are plain functions. Call them with a stand-in event:

```python
from types import SimpleNamespace

async def _noop():
    pass

async def test_echo_replies(monkeypatch):
    replies = []

    fake_event = SimpleNamespace(
        text="hello",
        chat_id="g0test",
        reply=lambda text: replies.append(text) or _noop(),
    )

    await echo(bot=object(), event=fake_event)

    assert replies == ["hello"]
```

For `async def reply(...)` handlers, make the stub awaitable:

```python
from types import SimpleNamespace

class FakeEvent:
    def __init__(self, text, chat_id="g0test"):
        self.text = text
        self.chat_id = chat_id
        self.replies = []

    async def reply(self, text):
        self.replies.append(text)
```

## Test routers without a token

```python
from darkob import Router

def test_routes_are_registered():
    router = Router()

    @router.command("start")
    async def start(bot, event): ...

    assert len(router) == 1
    assert router.routes[0].kind == "on_command"
```

## Test conversations

`MemoryStorage` makes FSM tests trivial and isolated:

```python
from darkob import FSMContext, MemoryStorage, StateFilter

async def test_address_flow():
    storage = MemoryStorage()
    ctx = FSMContext(storage, key="chat")

    await ctx.set_state("address")
    assert await StateFilter(storage, "address").evaluate(
        SimpleNamespace(chat_id="chat")
    )

    await ctx.update_data(address="Main St")
    assert await ctx.get_data() == {"address": "Main St"}
```

## Assert that nothing hits the network

Guard the socket layer in a test:

```python
import socket

def test_import_is_offline(monkeypatch):
    def boom(*args, **kwargs):
        raise AssertionError("network access")

    monkeypatch.setattr(socket.socket, "connect", boom)

    import darkob  # already imported in practice; use a subprocess for a real check
```

darkob itself checks this in a subprocess, which is the only reliable way
to catch import-time I/O.

## Testing filters

Filters are async predicates over an event-shaped object:

```python
from types import SimpleNamespace
from darkob.bot.filters import Text, IsGroup

async def test_text_filter():
    event = SimpleNamespace(original_data={"message": {"text": "hi there"}})
    assert await Text("hi").evaluate(event) is True
```

## Golden rules

1. Never let a test hit a real API.
2. Freeze time and randomness when asserting on retries.
3. Test the failure path as often as the happy path — that is where
   darkob's own bugs were found.


## `darkob.testing`

Ship-ready fakes, so a handler test needs no token, no network and no
hand-written stubs:

```python
from darkob.testing import FakeBot, make_message

async def test_echo(bot=None):
    bot = FakeBot()
    event = make_message(text="hi")

    await echo(bot, event)

    assert event.replies == ["hi"]
```

`FakeBot` records every call and returns an `{"status": "OK"}` payload:

```python
await bot.send_message("chat", "hi")

bot.called("send_message")          # True
bot.calls_to("send_message")        # [(("chat", "hi"), {})]
bot.last_call()[0]                  # "send_message"
bot.reset()                         # forget everything
```

`FakeEvent` records what a handler does to it:

```python
event = make_message(text="hello", chat_id="g0abc")
await event.reply("thanks")

event.replies    # ["thanks"]
event.edits      # []
event.deleted    # False
```

Both accept extra keyword attributes, so you can shape the event to match
your filters:

```python
event = make_message(text="hi", is_group=True)
```


---
# SOURCE: how-to/observe-in-production.md


Turn on darkob's in-process metrics, read them as a dict, and expose them to Prometheus without adding a metrics server dependency.

## Turn it on

```python
from darkob.metrics import enable_metrics, metrics

enable_metrics()          # off by default
bot.run()
```

`enable_metrics()` configures and enables the shared registry and returns
it. All arguments are keyword-only:

| Argument | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `prefix` | `"darkob"` | Prefix applied to every metric name when rendering |
| `histogram_capacity` | `512` | Samples kept per histogram for percentiles |
| `reset` | `True` | Clear anything recorded before enabling |

`disable_metrics()` turns instrumentation off again and keeps whatever was
already recorded.

!!! note "Import `metrics` from `darkob.metrics`"
    The registry instance is deliberately **not** re-exported from the
    package root: `from darkob import metrics` would be ambiguous with the
    module of the same name. Import the functions from the root, the
    instance from the module:

    ```python
    from darkob import enable_metrics          # function
    from darkob.metrics import metrics         # registry instance
    ```

## What gets recorded for you

| Metric | Kind | Recorded when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `darkob.updates` | counter | An update is received |
| `darkob.update.seconds` | histogram | Dispatch of one update finishes |
| `darkob.handlers.skipped` | counter | A handler's filters did not match |
| `darkob.handlers.called` | counter | A handler passed its filters |
| `darkob.handlers.errors` | counter | A handler raised |
| `darkob.api.requests` | counter | An HTTP call is issued |
| `darkob.api.errors` | counter | An HTTP call failed |
| `darkob.api.retries` | counter | A retry follows a failure |
| `darkob.api.ratelimited` | counter | The server throttled a call |
| `darkob.api.seconds` | histogram | Latency of one HTTP call |
| `darkob.queue.pending` | gauge | Messages waiting in a `SendQueue` |

!!! note "Where the counters fire"
    Both surfaces are instrumented. On `Messenger`/`Shad` the counters come
    from the client request loop and its dispatch path; on `Bot` they come
    from `Bot.request` and the polling/webhook funnel, so `darkob.api.*`,
    `darkob.updates` and the `darkob.handlers.*` counters all tick there too.

    `SendQueue` publishes `darkob.queue.pending` itself, on every enqueue,
    flush and drain — you do not have to poll it.

    This was not always true: 0.18.0 wired the `Bot` surface, which had been
    bypassing the instrumentation entirely because it owns a separate request
    path. If you are on an earlier build, set the gauge yourself:

    ```python
    metrics.set("darkob.queue.pending", queue.pending)
    ```

    Every counter, gauge and histogram you create yourself works the same way
    on both surfaces.

## Read a snapshot

```python
snapshot = metrics.snapshot()
```

```python
{
  "counters": {"darkob.api.requests": 1284},
  "gauges": {},
  "histograms": {
    "darkob.api.seconds": {
      "count": 1284, "sum": 23.5, "min": 0.004, "max": 2.1,
      "mean": 0.018, "p50": 0.012, "p95": 0.041, "p99": 0.5,
    }
  },
}
```

(Values shortened for readability.) `snapshot()` is plain JSON-safe data,
so `json.dumps(metrics.snapshot())` works as-is. Percentiles come from a
bounded ring buffer of the last `histogram_capacity` samples per histogram
— memory stays flat however long the bot runs, and the sort only happens
when you ask for a snapshot.

## Render the Prometheus text format

```python
print(metrics.render_prometheus())
```

```text
# TYPE darkob_api_requests counter
darkob_api_requests 1284
# TYPE darkob_api_seconds summary
darkob_api_seconds{quantile="0.5"} 0.012
darkob_api_seconds{quantile="0.95"} 0.041
darkob_api_seconds{quantile="0.99"} 0.5
darkob_api_seconds_count 1284
darkob_api_seconds_sum 23.5
```

Dots become underscores, the configured prefix is prepended once, counters
become `counter` lines, gauges `gauge` lines, and histograms become
`summary` metrics with `quantile` labels plus `_count` and `_sum`. Pass
`render_prometheus(prefix="mybot")` to change the prefix for one render.

## Scrape it with aiohttp

darkob's webhook server is created inside `bot.run()` and is not exposed,
so serve metrics on their own port:

```python title="metrics_server.py"
from aiohttp import web

from darkob.metrics import metrics


async def scrape(request):
    return web.Response(
        text=metrics.render_prometheus(),
        content_type="text/plain",
        charset="utf-8",
    )


app = web.Application()
app.router.add_get("/metrics", scrape)
web.run_app(app, host="127.0.0.1", port=9101)
```

```yaml title="prometheus.yml"
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: darkob
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["127.0.0.1:9101"]
```

Bind to `127.0.0.1` and let Prometheus reach it over a private network or
an authenticated proxy: metric names and label-less values are harmless,
but the endpoint still leaks your traffic volume.

## Record your own numbers

The same registry is public, so application metrics sit next to the
built-in ones:

```python
from darkob.metrics import metrics

metrics.increment("orders.created")
metrics.decrement("orders.queued")
metrics.set("workers.busy", 3)
metrics.adjust("workers.busy", -1)
metrics.observe("orders.total_seconds", 0.42)

with metrics.timer("orders.checkout"):
    await checkout()

@metrics.time_it("catalog.search")
async def search(query: str) -> list:
    ...
```

`time_it` handles sync and async callables, and uses
`module.qualname` when you pass no name.

!!! note "What 'off' actually costs"
    While the registry is disabled the library's own instrumentation costs
    one attribute read and a branch per hot-path call — it records nothing,
    which is why metrics are opt-in. Your own `metrics.increment(...)` calls
    are not guarded: they record whether or not you called
    `enable_metrics()` first.

# SOURCE: how-to/health-checks.md


Expose liveness and readiness probes so a container orchestrator restarts a wedged bot and stops routing traffic to one that cannot reach Rubika.

## Liveness versus readiness

A polling bot needs no health endpoint: if the process runs, it works. A
bot behind a webhook, in a container, or behind a load balancer does need
one, because "the process is up" and "the bot can do its job" are different
facts.

| Probe | Question | Failure means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **liveness** | Is this process still functioning? | Restart it |
| **readiness** | Should traffic be sent here? | Stop routing, keep running |

Only **critical readiness** checks can make a service unready. A failing
non-critical check marks the report `degraded` and still answers `200`: a
missing optional dependency should not get your pod killed.

## Register checks

```python
from darkob.health import HealthRegistry, queue_backlog_check, tcp_check

health = HealthRegistry()                     # default per-check timeout: 5s
health.add("api", tcp_check("messenger.rubika.ir", 443), kind="readiness")
health.add("outbox", queue_backlog_check(queue, max_pending=500),
           kind="readiness", critical=False)
health.add("loop", lambda: True, kind="liveness")
```

`add(name, check, *, kind="readiness", critical=True, timeout=None)`
returns the check unchanged, so it doubles as a decorator:

```python
@health.add("db")
async def check_db() -> bool:
    return await pool.ping()
```

| Argument | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | required | Identifier in the report |
| `check` | `None` | Callable; omit it to use `add` as a decorator |
| `kind` | `"readiness"` | `"readiness"` or `"liveness"` — anything else is a `ValueError` |
| `critical` | `True` | Whether a failing readiness check makes the service unready |
| `timeout` | `None` | Overrides the registry timeout for this check |

`remove(name)`, `clear()`, `names` and `len(health)` manage the registry.

## Writing a check

A check returns `True`, `False`, a string, or an awaitable of either. A
**string means "unhealthy"** and is used as the detail, which is the
cheapest way to say why:

```python
@health.add("quota")
async def quota_ok():
    left = await remaining_quota()
    return True if left > 100 else f"only {left} requests left"
```

darkob catches whatever a check raises and reports it as a failure
(`"TimeoutError: …"`), including timeouts, so one broken probe can never
take the endpoint down with it. Checks run concurrently.

!!! warning "Do not probe the API from a readiness check"
    A check that logs in or calls `getMe` spends your quota and can be
    throttled. Prefer a TCP connect, a queue depth, or a value your bot
    already tracks.

## The two ready-made checks

```python
from darkob.health import queue_backlog_check, tcp_check

tcp_check("messenger.rubika.ir", 443)          # port=443, timeout=2.0
queue_backlog_check(queue, max_pending=1000)   # accepts a SendQueue
```

`tcp_check(host, port=443, *, timeout=2.0)` opens a TCP connection and
closes it immediately: enough to separate "the network is gone" from "the
process is wedged", without authenticating.

`queue_backlog_check(queue, max_pending=1000)` reads `queue.pending`, and
falls back to `len(queue)` for any object without that attribute. A
`SendQueue` that keeps growing is the earliest sign that sends are failing.
Pair it with `critical=False`: a backlog should degrade, not restart.

## Read the report

```python
report = await health.report()          # or report("readiness") / report("liveness")
report.status        # "ok" | "degraded" | "down"
report.ok            # True when the service is usable
report.live, report.ready
report.http_status   # 200 or 503
report.to_dict()     # JSON-safe dict
report.to_json()     # compact JSON string
```

The body looks like this:

```json
{"status": "ok", "ok": true, "live": true, "ready": true, "duration": 0.004,
 "checks": [{"name": "api", "healthy": true, "detail": "ok",
             "kind": "readiness", "duration": 0.004}]}
```

`await health.ready()` and `await health.live()` are shortcuts returning a
single boolean.

| Situation | `status` | `ok` | HTTP |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Everything passes | `ok` | `True` | 200 |
| A non-critical readiness check fails | `degraded` | `True` | 200 |
| A critical readiness check fails | `down` | `False` | 503 |
| A liveness check fails | `down` | `False` | 503 |

A liveness failure also sets `live=False`; readiness only affects `ready`.

## Serve it

### aiohttp

```python title="health_server.py"
from aiohttp import web

from darkob.health import HealthRegistry, queue_backlog_check

health = HealthRegistry()
health.add("outbox", queue_backlog_check(queue, 500), critical=False)

app = web.Application()
app.router.add_get("/healthz", health.aiohttp_handler())
app.router.add_get("/livez", health.aiohttp_handler("/livez"))

web.run_app(app, host="127.0.0.1", port=8081)
```

`aiohttp_handler(path=None)` answers with `request.path` by default, so
pass the path explicitly when you mount the handler somewhere outside the
standard names below.

### Any ASGI framework

The registry maps paths itself:

| Paths | Probe |
| --- | --- |
| `/health`, `/healthz`, `/health/ready`, `/ready`, `/readyz` | readiness |
| `/health/live`, `/live`, `/livez`, `/health/liveness` | liveness |

`health.asgi_app()` returns a self-contained ASGI application for those
paths — it answers `GET` and `HEAD`, refuses other methods with `405`, and
returns `404` for unknown paths. Hand it to any server that accepts an ASGI
app. If your framework's router wants a request handler instead, return
the report yourself — three lines that work anywhere aiohttp does:

```python
from aiohttp import web

async def healthz(request):
    report = await health.report()
    return web.Response(
        text=report.to_json(),
        status=report.http_status,
        content_type="application/json",
    )
```

# SOURCE: how-to/write-a-plugin.md


Package cross-cutting behaviour — filtering, rewriting, error reporting — as a `Plugin` with a lifecycle instead of another handler.

## A plugin is a class and some metadata

```python title="plugins/anti_spam.py"
from darkob.plugin import Plugin, PluginMeta


class AntiSpam(Plugin):
    meta = PluginMeta(
        name="anti-spam",
        version="1.0.0",
        description="Drops messages that contain blocked words.",
        dependencies=(),
        default_config={"words": ["buy crypto"]},
    )

    async def setup(self) -> None:
        self.blocked = {w.lower() for w in self.get_config("words", [])}

    async def on_update(self, event):
        text = (event.text or "").lower()
        if any(word in text for word in self.blocked):
            return True      # consume: no handler sees this update
        return None          # let dispatch continue
```

`PluginMeta` is a frozen dataclass:

| Field | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | required | Identifier, lowercased on registration |
| `version` | `"1.0.0"` | Reported by `get_plugin_info` |
| `description` | `""` | Human-readable summary |
| `author` | `"Unknown"` | Reported by `get_plugin_info` |
| `homepage` | `None` | Reported by `get_plugin_info` |
| `dependencies` | `()` | Plugin names enabled before this one |
| `required_permissions` | `()` | Declarative only — **not** enforced by the manager |
| `default_config` | `{}` | Merged under the config you pass in |
| `enabled_by_default` | `False` | Picked up by `enable_defaults()` |

Without a `name`, the identifier falls back to the lowercased class name;
`register_plugin(MyPlugin, name="custom")` overrides both.

## Lifecycle and configuration

```python
async def setup(self) -> None:      # called by enable()
    ...
async def teardown(self) -> None:   # called by disable()
    ...
def configure(self, config: dict) -> dict:   # validate/rewrite config
    return config
self.get_config("words", [])        # one value
self.update_config({"words": []})   # merged over the defaults
self.is_ready                       # True between setup and teardown
```

A plugin receives its config at construction; `set_config()` on the manager
also applies to a live instance.

## The four hooks

| Hook | Signature | Return value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `on_update` | `(event)` | `True` consumes the update; `None`/`False` continues |
| `before_request` | `(action, data)` | A dict replaces the request body; `None` keeps it |
| `after_response` | `(action, data)` | A replacement payload; `None` keeps it |
| `on_error` | `(error, context)` | Ignored |

Every hook is a no-op in the base class, so a plugin that only implements
`setup()`/`teardown()` keeps working. At dispatch, only the hooks a plugin
actually **overrides** are called, in the order the plugins were enabled.

```python title="plugins/audit.py"
class Audit(Plugin):
    meta = PluginMeta(name="audit")

    def __init__(self, bot, *, config=None):
        super().__init__(bot, config=config)
        self.seen = []

    async def before_request(self, action, data):
        if action == "sendMessage":
            return {**data, "disable_notification": True}
        return None                           # keep the original body

    async def after_response(self, action, data):
        self.seen.append(action)
        return None                           # keep the payload

    async def on_error(self, error, context):
        print("failed:", type(error).__name__, context.get("action"))
```

!!! warning "`before_request` must return a dict"
    Anything else is reported to the hook-failure path and ignored, and the
    original body is sent, so a typo in a rewrite hook cannot silently
    corrupt every request — but it also means the failure is quiet unless
    you watch the logs.

## Register and enable

```python
from plugins.anti_spam import AntiSpam

bot = Bot(token="YOUR_BOT_TOKEN")

identifier = bot.plugin_manager.register_plugin(AntiSpam)   # "anti-spam"
plugin = await bot.plugin_manager.enable(identifier)        # instance
```

`Bot(...)` creates the manager for you, so registration is one call.

!!! note "Where the hooks actually fire"
    Both surfaces call all four hooks. On `Messenger`/`Shad` they run from the
    client's request and dispatch loop; on `Bot` they run from `Bot.request`
    and from `_safe_feed`, the funnel that polling and webhook updates both
    pass through.

    This was not always true. Until 0.18.0 the `Bot` surface had its own
    request path and dispatch loop that never invoked a hook, so a plugin
    written against the client worked on the userbot and silently did nothing
    on a bot. `tests/test_bot_instrumentation.py` now asserts the wiring on
    `Bot` specifically, because asserting it on the internal helper is what
    let the gap survive.

    A plugin can consume an update and stop dispatch below it:

    ```python
    async def on_update(self, event):
        if is_spam(event):
            return True      # no handler, and no ask(), will see it
        return None
    ```

`register_plugin` returns the normalised identifier and raises
`PluginDefinitionError` for a class that does not subclass `Plugin`, an
empty name, or a duplicate.

`enable()` returns the live instance and, on the way, enables the plugin's
`dependencies` first. A failure in `setup()` raises `PluginLoadError` and
leaves the plugin disabled; a circular dependency raises `PluginLoadError`
too.

```python
bot.plugin_manager.is_registered("anti-spam")   # True
bot.plugin_manager.is_enabled("anti-spam")      # True
bot.plugin_manager.enabled_plugins              # ["anti-spam"]
bot.plugin_manager.get_plugin("anti-spam")      # the instance
await bot.plugin_manager.disable("anti-spam")   # teardown, returns bool
await bot.plugin_manager.disable_all()
await bot.plugin_manager.reload("anti-spam")    # re-executes the file
```

`disable()` refuses while another enabled plugin depends on this one, and
returns `False` instead of raising.

## Failure isolation

A plugin that raises inside a hook is logged and skipped; the bot keeps
running. Turn that off when a plugin must fail closed — a security filter
that breaks should stop traffic, not vanish:

```python
from darkob.plugin import PluginManager

manager = PluginManager(bot, auto_discover=False, strict_hooks=True)
manager.register_plugin(AntiSpam)
await manager.enable("anti-spam")
```

With `strict_hooks=True` the hook's exception propagates out of
`run_on_update`, `apply_before_request`, `apply_after_response` or
`run_on_error` instead of being swallowed.

`PluginTester(MyPlugin, strict_hooks=True)` wires the strict manager for
you, which is the easiest way to assert that a hook *does* raise.

## Test it with `PluginTester`

`PluginTester` registers, enables and drives plugins against a
`FakeBot` — no token, no network:

```python title="tests/test_anti_spam.py"
from darkob.plugin import PluginTester
from darkob.testing import make_message
from plugins.anti_spam import AntiSpam


async def test_blocked_word_is_consumed():
    async with PluginTester(AntiSpam) as tester:
        assert await tester.on_update(make_message("buy crypto now")) is True
        assert await tester.on_update(make_message("hello")) is False
```

`PluginTester` can also drive the other three hooks — `before_request`,
`after_response`, `on_error` — plus `enabled` and `active`. Pass
`config={"anti-spam": {"words": ["spam"]}}` to override the meta defaults
before `setup()` runs.

## Discovery

`PluginManager(bot)` auto-discovers by default: it imports every `*.py` in
the `plugins/` directory next to your bot, and every entry point registered
under the `rubika.plugins` group. Pass `auto_discover=False` (or
`plugins_dir=None`) to keep enabling explicit.
